ss-rex-gambling-ships.story: The SS Rex was a floating casino anchored in Santa Monica Bay, off Los Angeles, in 1938 and 1939, one of several gambling ships that operated there from 1928. Gambling was illegal in California, but state power then stopped three miles from the coast and federal law did not forbid gambling at sea, so operators moored just past that limit and ferried customers out. Tony Cornero launched the Rex in 1938 and ran it day and night, with 1,000 to 3,000 gamblers aboard. District Attorney Buron Fitts arrested him and argued that Santa Monica Bay was an inland bay. On that view the three miles should be counted from a line drawn across the bay between Point Vicente and Point Dume, which would put the ship inside state waters. Cornero answered that the bay was only a bight, an open curve in the coast. Fitts won at first, but the ruling was overturned on appeal. In 1939 California Attorney General Earl Warren tried a different argument, that a state could stop a public nuisance even outside its jurisdiction. On 1 August 1939 authorities raided four ships. The Rex, which had no engines, blocked its landing platform and turned fire hoses on police boats. Cornero surrendered after eight days, saying he needed a haircut. A later court ruling closed the ships for good, and in 1948 President Truman signed a federal ban on gambling ships in US waters.
ss-rex-gambling-ships.mechanism: A coastal state's waters are measured from a legal line, and where that line crosses a bay can decide whether a ship is inside them. California also claimed it could stop a nuisance beyond its waters, and federal law later banned gambling ships in US waters outright.
ss-rex-gambling-ships.stopped_by: California Attorney General Earl Warren, whose officers raided the ships in 1939
ss-rex-gambling-ships.challenge: Cornero won on appeal over how to measure the bay, then lost to Warren's 1939 raids against the ships as a public nuisance

villa-vie-odyssey.story: The Villa Vie Odyssey was a former cruise ship turned into a floating home, with residents buying cabins and sailing the world for years at a time. Villa Vie Residences bought the Braemar from the cruise line Fred Olsen and sold cabins, called villas, for $99,999 and up plus a monthly fee, for the working life of the ship, which it put at 15 years or more. Its customers were mainly adventurous retirees and people who work online while travelling. The first voyage was planned to reach 425 ports in 147 countries. In summer 2024 the ship sat for months at the Harland & Wolff repair yard in Belfast, Northern Ireland, while the company worked on rudder shafts, steel and engines. A marketing manager said the firm had been humbled by what it takes to bring back a 30-year-old ship after four years out of service. It finally sailed on 30 September 2024. A year later a company press release claimed 46 countries, 138 ports and hundreds of full-time residents. It offered ownership from $129,999 and a lifetime plan from $99,999 called the Golden Passport, which is the name of a cruise plan and is not a travel document of any state. On 26 October 2026, at Sihanoukville in Cambodia, the chief executive told residents to leave because the company could not secure fuel. More than 200 residents, mostly Americans, went ashore. Chief executive Mikael Petterson blamed fuel prices that rose after the war with Iran began in late February, said payrolls had been met with borrowed money, and said the company planned to file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection. No filing had been reported by 29 October. The company never claimed to be a sovereign territory.
villa-vie-odyssey.mechanism: A residential ship keeps people away from any one country's daily control, but it still needs a flag state (the country whose registry and law it sails under), repair yards and permission from each port it enters.
villa-vie-odyssey.challenge: No government challenged it; it stopped in October 2026 for lack of fuel and money
villa-vie-odyssey.cost: Cabins from $99,999 in 2024 plus monthly fees, and from $129,999 by 2025
villa-vie-odyssey.why: Marked inhabited: the ship had hundreds of residents until October 2026, and the entry's own population field says so.

women-on-waves.story: Women on Waves is a Dutch group, founded by the doctor Rebecca Gomperts, that sails to countries with strict abortion laws and takes women out to international waters to give them abortion pills. It relies on a basic rule of the sea. A country's criminal law generally stops at the edge of its territorial sea, the belt of water reaching 12 nautical miles from the coast. Beyond that, on the high seas, a ship follows the law of its flag state, the country where it is registered. The group's ship is registered in the Netherlands and holds a permit from the Dutch Ministry of Health. Its first voyage, to Ireland in 2001, was cut short because it lacked a proper Dutch licence. In 2003 it sailed to Poland, which charged it with bringing in abortion drugs and dropped the charges four months later for lack of evidence. In 2004 two Portuguese warships blocked its ship, the Borndiep, from reaching the port of Figueira da Foz. The group took Portugal to the European Court of Human Rights, which ruled in February 2009 that Portugal had breached freedom of expression and assembly, and that lighter steps such as seizing the pills would have been enough. The group has also sailed to Spain, Morocco, Guatemala and Mexico. In Guatemala the army blocked the pier within 24 hours of docking. A law journal article notes that coastal states may still argue other grounds for jurisdiction over such a ship. In 2016 the group also used drones and speed boats to deliver pills to Northern Ireland. Its most recent reported ship campaign was to Mexico.
women-on-waves.mechanism: A ship registered in one country carries that country's law onto the high seas. In Women on Waves v Portugal (2009) the European Court of Human Rights limited how far a coastal state may go to keep such a ship out.
women-on-waves.stopped_by: Blocked at times by Portuguese warships and the Guatemalan army
women-on-waves.challenge: Won at the European Court of Human Rights, which found Portugal's 2004 blockade breached free expression
women-on-waves.recognition: Makes no claim to sovereignty; it uses the law of its Dutch flag

china-balloon-2023.story: On 4 February 2023 US F-22 fighter jets shot down a Chinese high-altitude balloon over the Atlantic off South Carolina. According to US military officials it was then between 60,000 and 65,000 feet up, about 20 kilometres, above US territorial waters. China called this unlawful force against a civil aircraft. The United States said the balloon was a military surveillance craft violating its sovereignty. The dispute matters here because it shows what the law treats a craft at that height as being. An analysis from Leiden Law School in the Netherlands reasoned that a balloon counts as an aircraft under the 1944 Chicago Convention, the main treaty on international flying. Article 1 of that treaty gives each country full control of the air above its land and territorial waters, and at 20 kilometres the balloon was in airspace and not in outer space, so flying there without permission breached US sovereignty. If the balloon was a civil aircraft, Article 3 bis and customary law limit the use of weapons against it. If it was a state aircraft, the convention does not apply and the general law on countermeasures, meaning steps taken in response to another state's breach, does. A Jakarta Post article noted that the International Telecommunication Union treats stations at 20 to 50 kilometres as high-altitude platforms, while no treaty sets where airspace ends. Debris was recovered from the Atlantic. Loon's internet balloons flew at around the same height, with the consent of the countries below.
china-balloon-2023.mechanism: Countries treat the lower stratosphere as their own airspace, and the United States used force to defend that claim at about 20 kilometres up.
china-balloon-2023.laws: The Chicago Convention on international flying, as applied by legal commentators
china-balloon-2023.founder: China, as operator of the balloon

cloud-nine.story: Cloud Nine was a design for cities floating in the sky, drawn up around 1960 by the American architect Buckminster Fuller and his partner Shoji Sadao. Their photocollage, Project for Floating Cloud Structures, showed several thousand people living inside enclosed spheres a mile wide, drifting above the ground. Fuller's reasoning was geometric. His geodesic spheres are frames built from triangles, and a sphere's shell grows more slowly than the volume of air it holds. At a mile across, he argued, the structure weighs little compared with the air inside, so warming that air by one degree would lift the whole sphere. A sheet of polyethylene would cover the frame. The sphere could be tethered, left to float, or steered to follow the weather or to serve as emergency shelter. Nothing was built and no government was consulted, so no regulator ever ruled on it. The law it would have met is the 1944 Chicago Convention, the treaty under which each country has full control of the air above its land. A 2023 analysis from Leiden Law School treats even a high-altitude balloon as an aircraft under that treaty, which suggests a drifting city would need permission from each country below it.
cloud-nine.mechanism: A home floating in the atmosphere is still in the airspace of the country beneath it, so leaving the ground does not take it outside that country's control.

jp-aerospace-dark-sky-station.story: JP Aerospace is a volunteer American group that wants to reach orbit by airship, with a permanently inhabited floating base high over the Earth on the way. Its founder, the engineer John Powell, has worked on high-altitude balloons and rockets since 1979. The plan, called Airship to Orbit, has three stages. Sturdy airships carry people and cargo from the ground to a floating base called a Dark Sky Station. Lighter craft built for thin air then climb from the base to orbit. The technology news site The Register described the stations as mile-wide platforms at 140,000 feet carrying telecoms equipment and tourist hotels, while Powell told MSNBC in 2004 that the full-size station in his plan was two miles across. The hardware built so far is small. For the US Air Force the group made a 175-foot V-shaped airship called Ascender at a cost of about $500,000. On 22 October 2011 an uncrewed craft called Tandem manoeuvred under power at 95,085 feet above Nevada, and a small prototype station has flown using helium balloons and carbon-fibre frames. Nobody has lived on any of it, and the group makes no claim to sovereignty. At 140,000 feet, about 43 kilometres, a station would sit well below both the 100-kilometre and 80-kilometre lines proposed as the edge of space.
jp-aerospace-dark-sky-station.mechanism: A platform 43 kilometres up would be below every proposed boundary of outer space, so it would sit in the airspace of whichever country lay beneath it.
jp-aerospace-dark-sky-station.cost: About $500,000 to build the 175-foot Ascender test airship, according to a US Air Force officer in 2004

karman-line-debate.story: International law has no agreed height at which a country's airspace ends and outer space begins. Airspace belongs to the country below, and outer space belongs to no country, yet neither the 1944 Chicago Convention on flying nor the 1967 Outer Space Treaty says where one becomes the other. The figure most often used is the Karman line at 100 kilometres, named after the engineer Theodore von Karman. Lausanne-based FAI, the international body that keeps air-sport records, uses it to separate aeronautics from astronautics. Others differ. The US armed forces call anyone who has flown above 50 miles, about 80 kilometres, an astronaut, and NASA changed from the 100-kilometre figure to match them in 2005. In 2018 the astronomer Jonathan McDowell published a paper in the journal Acta Astronautica proposing 80 kilometres as better suited to the physics and to the orbits actually flown. Another proposal sets the boundary at the lowest point a satellite can reach in orbit, with no fixed number. Legal writers describe two camps. The spatial camp wants a fixed height, and the functional camp would classify an object by what it does. The question matters to anyone trying to set up a place beyond national control, because the answer decides which body of law applies between roughly 20 and 100 kilometres up, and the matter remains unsettled.
karman-line-debate.mechanism: No treaty fixes the boundary between national airspace and outer space, so the band between the highest aircraft and the lowest satellites has no settled legal rules and is open to competing claims.
karman-line-debate.founder: No founder; a long-running disagreement among states, agencies and scientists

loon-stratosphere.story: Loon was a project to bring internet access to remote areas using balloons that carried mobile network equipment about 20 kilometres up, steered by choosing among high-altitude winds. It began in 2011 at Google's experimental lab, Google X, and later became a separate company under Google's parent, Alphabet. Service reached Sri Lanka in 2015 and Puerto Rico in 2017 after Hurricane Maria. Its work in Kenya shows how the law applied at that height. Loon signed a contract with the operator Telkom Kenya in July 2018, then waited until March 2020 for the Kenyan government's formal approval to fly in the stratosphere above the country. Because balloons drift, Loon also signed an airspace agreement with neighbouring Uganda, and a company spokesperson told Reuters the balloons might pass above Uganda while serving Kenya. Launches took place in the United States, and the balloons navigated across to Africa. In January 2021 Alphabet announced it was closing Loon, and an account on the site Hackaday points to weak finances and customers in poor areas who could not bring in enough income. No country ever had to challenge Loon, because even at 20 kilometres, with no people on board and a large US company behind it, it asked each country along its path for consent.
loon-stratosphere.mechanism: Loon treated the stratosphere as national airspace by getting approval from each country its balloons might drift over, even at 20 kilometres up.
loon-stratosphere.stopped_by: Alphabet, which closed the company in 2021 because it lacked a viable business
loon-stratosphere.laws: Flight approvals obtained from each country
loon-stratosphere.challenge: Never challenged, because it asked each country for permission
loon-stratosphere.recognition: Approved by Kenya in 2020; overflight deal with Uganda reported in 2019

bantustans-transkei-bophuthatswana.story: Bantustans, also called homelands, were territories that South Africa's white-minority government set aside for black South Africans under apartheid, its system of racial separation. Four of them were declared independent countries, though no other government accepted this. The homeland policy was a way to strip black people of their place in South Africa. Hendrik Verwoerd, first as minister for native affairs and then as prime minister, built it up, and the Bantu Self-Government Act of 1959 set out a plan for homelands to become self-governing and then nominally independent. The Bantu Homelands Citizenship Act of 1970 declared black South Africans to be citizens of these homelands, which took away their South African citizenship and the few rights it still gave them. South Africa then declared four homelands independent, Transkei in 1976, Bophuthatswana in 1977, Venda in 1979 and Ciskei in 1981. Transkei served as the testing ground for the policy. Anti-apartheid movements and every other government refused to recognise these declarations. In 1985 President P. W. Botha said black people in South Africa proper would no longer lose their citizenship in this way, and that citizens of the independent homelands could reapply for it. The Interim Constitution that came with the end of apartheid in 1994 effectively abolished the Bantustans, and they were absorbed back into South Africa. Bophuthatswana's former leader Lucas Mangope later led a party that contested that ending.
bantustans-transkei-bophuthatswana.mechanism: Recognition means other states accepting a place as a state. South Africa granted these homelands independence to serve its own policy, and because no other state accepted them, they never counted as countries in international law.
bantustans-transkei-bophuthatswana.recognition: South Africa only; no other government
bantustans-transkei-bophuthatswana.laws: Homeland constitutions set up under South African laws
bantustans-transkei-bophuthatswana.stopped_by: End of apartheid and the Interim Constitution of 1994

denard-comoros.story: Bob Denard was a French mercenary, a soldier for hire, who took part in four attempts to change the government of the Comoros, a group of islands in the Indian Ocean, between 1975 and 1995. For long periods he was the real military power there. He often worked in support of France's influence in its former African colonies. On the orders of Jacques Foccart, President de Gaulle's adviser on Africa, he removed President Ahmed Abdallah in 1975, just after Abdallah had declared the islands independent. On 13 May 1978 he returned with 43 men, backed by the government of Rhodesia, and overthrew the new leader, Ali Soilih, who was killed on 29 May. The official account that he was shot while trying to escape is not generally believed. Abdallah came back as president, and for 11 years Denard ran his 500-strong presidential guard, became a citizen and acquired hotels and land. In 1989 Abdallah was shot in his office, allegedly by a military officer, and Denard agreed to leave after talks with French representatives. On 27 September 1995 he landed again with 30 to 33 men against President Djohar. The French army ended the attempt on 4 October, and he surrendered. A French court gave him a five-year suspended sentence in June 2006. On appeal in July 2007 this became four years with three suspended, which he never served because of poor health. Witnesses at the trial said French intelligence had supported him. He died in October 2007.
denard-comoros.mechanism: A small armed force can take over the government of a weak state, but Denard kept control only while France, the strongest outside power in the region, allowed it.
denard-comoros.challenge: Removed by French military intervention, then tried in French courts
denard-comoros.recognition: Held power through a recognised president of the Comoros

free-state-project.story: The Free State Project is an American movement that asks people who favour very limited government, known as libertarians, to move to New Hampshire so that they can change its politics. It began in 2001 when Jason Sorens, then a Yale graduate student, published an article in The Libertarian Enterprise, in an issue titled "Let's Secede!". He proposed forming an independent libertarian nation or, failing that, winning concessions from the US government. Sorens calculated that 20,000 libertarians moving to one small state could change it. After a mixed response he soon backed away from secession, saying it was not part of the project's approach, although it still matters to many members. Members chose New Hampshire in 2003 and signed a pledge to move within five years of the sign-up count reaching 20,000, which it did on 3 February 2016. By May 2022 about 6,232 people had moved. In the 2017 to 2018 term, Free Staters held 17 of the 400 seats in the state House of Representatives. In 2026 the former executive director Carla Gericke formed a movement called NH Exit Now, which calls for secession. Its website claims that 42% of voters favoured a ballot question in 2022, a figure that comes from the group itself. New Hampshire remains a US state.
free-state-project.mechanism: People who move to a state can vote and win seats there, but that gives them no legal way to take the state out of the United States.
free-state-project.pop: About 6,232 people had moved by May 2022
free-state-project.why: "Let's Secede!" was the title of the journal issue. Sorens's article was called "Announcement: The Free State Project", per the Wikipedia article.

grafton-free-town-project.story: The Free Town Project was an attempt by libertarians, who favour very limited government, to take over the politics of Grafton, a small town in New Hampshire. It was started in 2004 by a splinter group from the Free State Project, the larger movement that had just picked New Hampshire as the state to move to. Grafton attracted them because it had no zoning laws, which control how land may be used, and a very low property tax. It was also home to John Babiarz, a Libertarian Party figure who had twice run for governor. No records were kept of how many came, but the population rose from 1,138 in 2000 to 1,340 in 2010, with nearly all the newcomers men. Participants lived in yurts, recreational vehicles, trailers, tents and shipping containers. They voted through changes that included a 30% cut in the already small town budget and removing funding for the county's senior citizens' council. Lawsuits they filed to set legal precedents raised the town's costs. A book by Matt Hongoltz-Hetling linked the group to rising bear activity after attacks in the area, while the state's bear biologist said in 2023 that nothing suggested the bear population had spiked. Grafton remains an ordinary New Hampshire town.
grafton-free-town-project.mechanism: Newcomers can change a small town's budget through ordinary votes, but state and federal law continue to apply to everything there.
grafton-free-town-project.founder: A splinter group from the Free State Project

marinaleda.story: Marinaleda is a farming town of about 2,562 people in the province of Seville, southern Spain, known for running its land and housing along collective lines. Its people were mostly landless day labourers working for large landowners, and their campaign, under the slogan "Land to those who work on it", aimed to win land and better pay. A local group, the Workers' Unity Collective, won 9 of the 11 council seats in Spain's first local elections after the Franco dictatorship, in 1979, and its leader Juan Manuel Sánchez Gordillo stayed mayor until 2023. In 1980, 700 people held a 13-day hunger strike over pay. In 1984 residents occupied the Cordobilla marsh for 30 days to demand irrigation for El Humoso, a farm owned by the Duke of Infantado. In 1991, 1,200 hectares of that farm were handed over for local use. A cooperative founded in 1997 farms the land, and a food plant followed three years later. People who build their own houses pay no more than 15 euros a month. Critics say almost 66% of the town's income comes from higher levels of government, while the same source says it received about 6.61% less than the regional average in 2011. Marinaleda remains an ordinary Spanish municipality under Spanish law.
marinaleda.mechanism: A town can reorganise land and housing through elected office and pressure on the national government without leaving the country or its law.
marinaleda.founder: Juan Manuel Sánchez Gordillo and the Workers' Unity Collective

operation-red-dog-dominica.story: Operation Red Dog was a failed 1981 plot by white supremacists to overthrow the government of Dominica, a small Caribbean island country led by Prime Minister Eugenia Charles, and put former prime minister Patrick John back in power. Those involved included the long-time Ku Klux Klan member Mike Perdue, the German-Canadian Nazi Wolfgang Droege, the American white nationalist Don Black and the plot leader Sydney Burnett-Alleyne. Perdue first aimed at Grenada and hoped to set up lucrative businesses on the island he seized, then changed the target to Dominica. He later testified that he got $10,000 from a lawyer and used $70,000 collected from businessmen for weapons, dynamite and scouting trips. The plan was to sail to Dominica and meet John and an armed group there. In February 1981 the original captain and crew backed out, so Perdue approached another captain, Michael Howell, telling him the CIA needed his boat. Howell went to the US Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms (ATF), the federal agency that enforces gun laws. John was arrested in Dominica on 25 April. On 27 April, Droege and eight other men were arrested at a marina in New Orleans as they prepared to board, with automatic weapons, dynamite and a Nazi flag. Three undercover agents were in the group, and nobody was hurt.
operation-red-dog-dominica.mechanism: Plotters who need boats and guns must get them somewhere, and that puts them under another country's law. One boat captain's report to US agents stopped this plot before it left New Orleans.
operation-red-dog-dominica.stopped_by: US Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms, after a boat captain reported the plot
operation-red-dog-dominica.cost: About $70,000 collected for weapons and scouting trips

rajneeshpuram-antelope.story: Rajneeshpuram was a city built by followers of the Indian spiritual teacher Bhagwan Shree Rajneesh on a huge ranch in central Oregon in the 1980s. In 1981 they bought the 64,281-acre Big Muddy Ranch for $5.75 million, and within three years they had built a city of up to 7,000 people with its own police, fire service, airstrip and post office. Ma Anand Sheela, Rajneesh's secretary, acted as the commune's leader in practice. Antelope, the nearest town, had under 60 people. As more followers moved in, Antelope's residents voted in April 1982 on dissolving their town to avoid a takeover, and the followers had enough votes to defeat the plan. In May 1982 the ranch voted to become a city in its own right. Oregon's attorney general argued that the city merged church and state, and the group 1000 Friends of Oregon argued that it broke land-use law. In 1984 some leaders deliberately spread disease in an attempt to lower turnout in county elections, sickening 751 people and sending 45 to hospital. A plot to kill the US attorney for Oregon followed. Rajneesh was accused of immigration violations and entered a plea in which he did not admit guilt, agreeing to leave the country, and the commune broke up in 1985. A federal judge ruled against the city that year, too late to matter, and Oregon courts later upheld it. The ranch was sold in 1988 at a sheriff's auction for $4.5 million and is now a camp run by the Christian group Young Life.
rajneeshpuram-antelope.mechanism: Moving enough voters into a small area can legally win control of its local government, but state and federal criminal law continue to apply to those who hold it.
rajneeshpuram-antelope.stopped_by: Criminal prosecutions and the leader's plea deal
rajneeshpuram-antelope.laws: Legally incorporated as a city under Oregon law
rajneeshpuram-antelope.challenge: A federal judge ruled against it in 1985; Oregon courts later upheld it, after it had emptied

seychelles-1981-coup.story: In November 1981 a group of mercenaries, soldiers for hire, led by Mike Hoare tried to overthrow the government of Seychelles, an island country in the Indian Ocean, with encouragement from apartheid South Africa. Seychelles became independent in 1976 with James Mancham as president and France-Albert René as prime minister. In 1977 René's supporters seized power while Mancham was in London, and René became president. Mancham then sought South African help to return, and he was directed to Hoare, a veteran of mercenary wars in the Congo. Hoare advised raising $5 million but only $300,000 was found. On 25 November, 53 men took part. Nine went ahead, and 44 arrived at the international airport disguised as rugby players and members of a beer-drinking charity club, with weapons in their luggage. A security officer searching one man's bag found an AK-47, and the alarm went up. After a long gunfight in which one soldier and one mercenary died, most of the mercenaries hijacked an Air India airliner to Durban in South Africa. South Africa did not charge them with attempting a coup, only with aviation offences. Most were freed at first and charged later, and 34 of them served about four months. Hoare's sentence was ten years in Wikipedia's account and 20 in the Irish Times obituary, and he was released in May 1985 under an amnesty after about three years. A Seychelles court sentenced four captured men to death on 6 July 1982 and two others to prison. All six were pardoned after talks and a $3 million payment to René. A UN inquiry and South Africa's later Truth and Reconciliation Commission condemned South Africa's role, although a South African judge cleared the government at the time.
seychelles-1981-coup.mechanism: A plot against a recognised government depends on its secrecy, and this one was exposed by one bag search at the airport. South Africa, which encouraged it, later faced international condemnation.
seychelles-1981-coup.stopped_by: An airport security search and Seychelles forces
seychelles-1981-coup.founder: Mike Hoare, with South African government encouragement
seychelles-1981-coup.why: The earlier text said only eight of 43 accused were charged. Wikipedia's account has 45 men flying to Durban, five charged at first, and later trials ending with Hoare, seven others and 34 more all sentenced.

slab-city.story: Slab City is an off-the-grid camp in the desert of Imperial County, southern California, whose residents call it "the last free place". It has no local government. It takes its name from the concrete slabs left behind when the US Marines dismantled Camp Dunlap, a 631-acre training base opened in 1942. All the buildings were gone by 1956. In 1961 the Department of Defense passed the land to California by a quitclaim deed, a transfer with no promises about the title. Drifters and then owners of recreational vehicles came for the free camping. The Washington Post reported in 2020 that the population might reach 4,000 in winter, when retirees arrive to escape the cold, and fall to about 150 in summer. Reports conflict on who owns the land. Some say the state of California, and others from 1993 say a building contractor. In 2015 residents formed a community group to try to prevent a sale. As of 2021 California had not decided to sell, and its State Lands Commission was considering an appraisal and a clean-up of military waste. California and US law still apply to the camp, though they are largely not enforced there.
slab-city.mechanism: When a government does not enforce its rules, people can live freely on public land, but this lasts only as long as the owner leaves them alone.
slab-city.founder: No founder; squatters and winter visitors

wonga-coup-equatorial-guinea.story: The Wonga Coup was a failed 2004 plot by foreign mercenaries, soldiers for hire, to overthrow Teodoro Obiang, president of the oil-rich African country of Equatorial Guinea, and replace him with the exiled politician Severo Moto. It was organised by mainly British financiers. Prosecutors said Moto offered the group $1.8 million and oil rights. On 7 March 2004 police at Harare airport in Zimbabwe impounded a Boeing 727 from South Africa carrying three crew and 64 former soldiers. They arrested the former British special forces officer Simon Mann by the runway as he waited for arms to be loaded. Mann said the weapons were for guarding diamond mines in Congo. On 9 March Nick du Toit and 14 others were arrested in Equatorial Guinea, and du Toit testified that Mann had recruited him to install Moto. The name comes from a letter Mann wrote from prison asking for "a large splodge of wonga", British slang for money. On 13 January 2005 Mark Thatcher, son of the former British prime minister Margaret Thatcher, pleaded guilty in South Africa to attempting to breach its anti-mercenary law by agreeing to charter a helicopter he suspected might be used for mercenary activity. Al Jazeera reported he had paid $275,000 for the charter. He was fined 3 million rand, about $500,000, and given a four-year prison term suspended for five years. Mann served three years in Zimbabwe and was then extradited to Equatorial Guinea, where he was sentenced in 2008 to more than 34 years. President Obiang pardoned him on 2 November 2009 and he returned to England.
wonga-coup-equatorial-guinea.mechanism: A privately funded armed takeover has to pass through other countries on its way, and this one was stopped at an airport in Zimbabwe. One backer was then convicted under South Africa's law against mercenary activity.
wonga-coup-equatorial-guinea.cost: $180,000 deposit paid for arms; $275,000 from Mark Thatcher for a helicopter charter

bir-tawil-kingdom-of-north-sudan.story: Bir Tawil is a stretch of 2,060 square kilometres of desert on the border between Egypt and Sudan that neither country claims, and in 2014 an American farmer declared it a kingdom. Its odd status comes from two lines the British drew when they controlled the region. In 1899 they drew a straight border along the 22nd parallel. In 1902 they drew an administrative line that followed how local tribes used the land. Egypt relies on the first line and Sudan on the second, because each line gives that country the larger Hala'ib Triangle. Under either country's position, Bir Tawil belongs to the other, so nobody claims it. On 16 June 2014, his daughter's seventh birthday, Virginia farmer Jeremiah Heaton planted a blue flag there and declared the Kingdom of North Sudan so that she could be a princess. He said he asked for permission in Cairo to make the trip. He later applied for observer status at the United Nations, offered honorary titles for $25 and offered the right to name a capital city for $1.75 million. Noam Leshem, a geographer at Durham University, told Al Jazeera that the land's status is ambiguous and that tribes still use it. No government has recognised the kingdom, meaning none has accepted it as a state, and no one has settled there.
bir-tawil-kingdom-of-north-sudan.mechanism: This case tests whether a private person can acquire land that no government claims. International law allows only states to take terra nullius (land belonging to no state), so Heaton's flag and website gained him no legal title.
bir-tawil-kingdom-of-north-sudan.pop: No permanent population; miners and tribes pass through
bir-tawil-kingdom-of-north-sudan.challenge: Never tested by any state, in court or on the ground
bir-tawil-kingdom-of-north-sudan.recognition: None. An application for UN observer status was filed, and no government recognised it
bir-tawil-kingdom-of-north-sudan.cost: Heaton estimated at least $2 billion to start the project and sought up to $45 million online

bir-tawil-later-claimants.story: After the American farmer Jeremiah Heaton claimed Bir Tawil, an unclaimed strip of desert between Egypt and Sudan, in 2014, several other people declared their own states on the same land. In November 2017 Suyash Dixit, a 24-year-old businessman from Indore in India, flew from Cairo to Abu Simbel, drove in on 4 November, planted sunflower seeds and declared the Kingdom of Dixit, asking the United Nations for recognition. A day later the Russian Dmitry Zhikharev announced a Kingdom of Middle Earth, accused Heaton and Dixit of faking their visits, and said he had declared himself ruler in December 2014. In September 2019 a group naming the Michigan businesswoman Nadera Nassif as prime minister announced a Kingdom of the Yellow Mountain. Most claims were made online from elsewhere. The London barrister Dwain Coward told the magazine VICE he had set up a company in Sudan and sent terms to tribal chiefs, because gold miners using mercury were damaging the land. VICE reports that the only people working there are migrants from Sudan who dig for gold and sell it in Khartoum. No government or international body has recognised any of these claims.
bir-tawil-later-claimants.mechanism: Private people who claim the same land have no court to settle it between them, because only states can hold title to territory in international law and no state is involved here.
bir-tawil-later-claimants.pop: No residents; small-scale gold miners work the area seasonally

clipperton-arbitration.story: Clipperton is an uninhabited coral atoll in the eastern Pacific Ocean, and the dispute between France and Mexico over who owned it produced an important ruling on how a state can claim empty land. On 17 November 1858 the French naval lieutenant Victor le Coat de Kerwéguen, on a merchant ship half a mile offshore, proclaimed French sovereignty over it. A boat landed a few men, nobody left any sign of possession, and notice was sent to the Hawaiian government and printed in a Honolulu newspaper. Nothing further happened until 1897, when France found three people collecting guano, bird droppings used as fertiliser, for an American company. A Mexican gunboat arrived that December and replaced the American flag with Mexico's, and Mexico claimed the island as an inheritance from Spain. On 2 March 1909 the two countries agreed to arbitration, meaning they would let a chosen judge decide and accept the result, and they picked King Victor Emmanuel III of Italy. His award of 28 January 1931 found Mexico had not proved it held the island first, so in 1858 it was territorium nullius, land belonging to no state. Physical possession is normally required, he said, but on a completely uninhabited island a state's arrival can complete it at once. France lost nothing through 39 years of inaction, because it never intended to give the island up. Clipperton remains French territory and has no permanent residents.
clipperton-arbitration.mechanism: On a completely uninhabited territory, a state's clear intention, public notice and a brief presence can be enough to gain ownership, and later absence does not lose it unless the state means to abandon the land.
clipperton-arbitration.stopped_by: King Victor Emmanuel III of Italy, who as arbitrator awarded the island to France
clipperton-arbitration.pop: No stable population; three guano collectors in 1897
clipperton-arbitration.recognition: Both countries promised in advance to accept the award

couto-misto.story: Couto Misto was a group of three villages on the border of Spain and Portugal that governed itself for centuries, belonging fully to neither kingdom. The villages, Santiago de Rubiás, Rubiás and Meaus, lie in what is now the province of Ourense in Galicia, and a small uninhabited strip went with them. A couto was a medieval district marked by boundary stones and exempt from the king's authority, with its own economic and legal arrangements. Through overlapping feudal ties, this one escaped control by both crowns. Its origin is unclear, and one source dates it to the 10th century. Portugal abolished its coutos between 1692 and 1790, after which this one was also free of feudal ties and ran in practice as an independent state. It covered about 26.7 square kilometres and had about 1,000 people by an estimate from 1859. Residents paid no tax to either country, did not serve in either army, could grant asylum to outsiders and could refuse entry to foreign troops. Decisions came from an assembly of the people. The Treaty of Lisbon, dated 29 September 1864, divided the territory, with Spain taking the three villages and most of the land and Portugal taking the uninhabited strip. The takeover was completed in 1868.
couto-misto.mechanism: Long custom can produce working self-rule, but custom gives no protection once the neighbouring states agree by treaty to end it.
couto-misto.laws: An assembly of the people; right to grant asylum and to refuse foreign troops
couto-misto.challenge: Lasted until its two neighbours divided it by treaty

free-republic-of-verdis.story: Verdis is a self-declared state on a 128-acre strip of forest and marsh on the Danube river, between Croatia and Serbia, in an area known as Pocket 3. It exists as a claim because the two countries disagree about their river border and neither claims this piece. It is roughly the size of Vatican City. Daniel Jackson, born in Australia to British parents, had the idea at about age 14 and helped declare the state in 2019, after finding the plot through people he met online. He said it was meant as a neutral base for humanitarian groups, and that Liberland, a similar claim nearby, partly inspired it. He told NBC the group planted a flag in 2023 and did survey work. In October 2023 settlers tried to set up a permanent camp. Jackson said Croatian authorities destroyed it within days, arrested the group and told them to leave or be deported. He received a permanent ban from Croatia and the others received three-month bans. He now runs the project from Dover in England and says he plans a legal fight. Verdis had received about 15,000 citizenship applications at $16 each and had accepted about 350 to 400. No government recognises Verdis as a state.
free-republic-of-verdis.mechanism: Croatia physically controls the river bank, and that decides who may stay there, whoever may hold title on paper. Liberland met the same result on a larger scale.
free-republic-of-verdis.pop: None; a settlement lasted a few days in October 2023
free-republic-of-verdis.passports: About 350 to 400 issued to accepted applicants; Jackson says some have been used at borders
free-republic-of-verdis.laws: Founders set the rules for citizenship
free-republic-of-verdis.challenge: Failed on the ground, with settlers arrested and the founder banned from Croatia for life

free-state-of-bottleneck.story: The Free State of Bottleneck was a tiny area on the Rhine river in western Germany that ran itself from 1919 to 1920 after a quirk in Allied occupation maps cut it off from the rest of the country. After the First World War ended in 1918, Allied armies occupied Germany west of the Rhine and marked out three half-circles of 30 kilometres radius on the eastern bank, around Cologne, Koblenz and Mainz. The French and American half-circles did not quite meet. That left a narrow strip holding the Wisper valley, the towns of Lorch and Kaub and several villages. With occupied zones on two sides, the Rhine to the south-west and no road or railway to the north-east, the area was cut off from Germany and its government. Locals declared a free state on 10 January 1919, named after its bottleneck shape on the map. About 17,000 people lived there. Lorch was the capital, and its mayor, Edmund Pnischeck, was elected president. Goods and post came in mostly by smuggling, and once a French coal train was hijacked and the coal shared out for heating. The territory issued its own emergency money and passports. Its self-rule ended on 1 July 1920, after the German army put down the Ruhr uprising, and the area returned to the Prussian province of Hesse-Nassau. A 1923 end date, tied to the French occupation of the Ruhr, also circulates, but Pnischeck called it nonsense. The area is now part of the Rhine Gorge World Heritage Site.
free-state-of-bottleneck.mechanism: An error in drawing a military map can leave people outside any working government, and in this case they set up their own administration to run things until Germany took the area back.
free-state-of-bottleneck.stopped_by: Self-rule ended on 1 July 1920, after the German army put down the Ruhr uprising
free-state-of-bottleneck.currency: Local emergency money printed by the territory
free-state-of-bottleneck.challenge: Ended by events, with no contest
free-state-of-bottleneck.laws: Local administration under an elected president

island-of-palmas.story: Palmas, now called Miangas and part of Indonesia, is an island about 2.6 kilometres long between the Philippines and Indonesia, and a dispute over it produced one of the best-known rulings on how countries gain territory. In 1898 Spain gave the Philippines to the United States by a treaty whose boundaries took in Palmas. In 1906 the United States found that the Netherlands, then the colonial power in what is now Indonesia, also claimed it. On 23 January 1925 the two countries agreed to binding arbitration, meaning they would accept a chosen judge's decision, and the Swiss lawyer Max Huber acted as sole arbitrator. The United States argued that Spain had discovered the island, that the island lay close to the Philippines, and that it had inherited Spain's rights. Huber decided on 4 April 1928. He wrote that discovering land gives at most an inchoate title, a starting claim that must be completed by actual possession within a reasonable time. He rejected contiguity, the idea that being nearby is enough to give ownership. He held that the continuous and peaceful display of the functions of a state is as good as a title, and the Dutch had shown this from 1700 to 1906. The whole island was therefore Dutch territory, and it passed later to Indonesia.
island-of-palmas.mechanism: A country gains title to territory by actually governing it continuously and peacefully. Discovering it or being close to it does not beat that.
island-of-palmas.founder: Dispute between the United States and the Netherlands
island-of-palmas.stopped_by: Arbitrator Max Huber, sitting under the Permanent Court of Arbitration

islands-of-refreshment.story: The Islands of Refreshment was the name Jonathan Lambert, an American sailor from Salem, Massachusetts, gave to the Tristan da Cunha islands in the South Atlantic when he declared them his own. These remote islands then had no permanent residents. Lambert arrived on the whaler Grand Turk in December 1810, or January 1811 by another account, with two other men, later joined by a fourth. He declared himself Lord and Prince of Tristan da Cunha and its two neighbouring islands, Inaccessible and Nightingale, and the islands his property. He made his living by hunting seals and selling their oil to passing ships. Lambert drowned near Inaccessible Island on 27 May 1812, with the sailor Andrew Millet. By the end of that year only one of the four men, Tommaso Corri from Livorno in Italy, was still alive, and he stayed on as a farmer. On 14 August 1816 Britain annexed the islands by sending a garrison, because it wanted to stop them being used as a base to free Napoleon from his prison on Saint Helena, and to deter the United States, whose navy had used them in the War of 1812. The garrison left in 1817, but some of its members stayed and started the community that still lives there. Tristan da Cunha remains a British territory, with 243 people in 2021.
islands-of-refreshment.mechanism: Living on an unclaimed island and declaring it yours creates no title that other states must accept, and Britain took Tristan da Cunha by sending troops, without any dealings with the settler who had claimed it.
islands-of-refreshment.stopped_by: Lambert's death in 1812, then British annexation in 1816
islands-of-refreshment.why: The earlier text said Britain acted to prevent French or US use. Wikipedia gives the aim as stopping any attempt to free Napoleon from Saint Helena and deterring the US. Added that Lambert died in 1812, four years before the annexation.

kingdom-of-enclava.story: The Kingdom of Enclava was a self-declared state on a small plot on the border of Slovenia and Croatia, near the village of Brezovica pri Metliki. The border there is tangled, with a small Croatian enclave, a piece of one country surrounded by another, already sitting inside Slovenian land. In 2015 the Polish tourist Piotr Wawrzynkiewicz read on Wikipedia that a small piece of land there was unclaimed, and he declared it a kingdom. Newspapers around the world reported the story. The Slovenian foreign ministry then said the plot was part of a territorial claim of its own, also claimed by Croatia, which was going before the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague. So an online reference page had called the land unclaimed while two governments were arguing over it in an international forum. On 29 June 2017 the court ruled that a disputed 2.4-hectare parcel beside the enclave belonged to Slovenia, which created a second Croatian enclave. Wawrzynkiewicz moved his project to an unclaimed area on the Croatia-Serbia border.
kingdom-of-enclava.mechanism: Land that looks unclaimed on a map may be under active dispute between states, and in that case the argument that it is terra nullius (land belonging to no state) fails as soon as those states speak.
kingdom-of-enclava.stopped_by: A Slovenian foreign ministry statement, then the 2017 arbitration ruling on the parcel
kingdom-of-enclava.challenge: Slovenia and Croatia both said the land was theirs; a 2017 ruling gave the parcel to Slovenia

kowloon-walled-city.story: Kowloon Walled City was an extremely crowded settlement in Hong Kong that for decades was largely outside the control of both Britain and China. It began as a Chinese fort, rebuilt in 1847 after Britain took Hong Kong Island. When Britain leased the neighbouring New Territories from China in 1898, the lease left out the fort, so it stayed a Chinese enclave, a piece of one country's land inside another's. In 1933 Hong Kong announced plans to clear it and rehouse 436 squatters. A further attempt to drive people out failed in 1948, and after that the British left most matters alone. Because neither government wanted to enforce its authority, refugees from the Chinese Civil War poured in. From the 1950s to the 1970s triads, Chinese criminal gangs, controlled the place, with gambling, prostitution and drug trafficking, until police raids in the 1970s reduced their power. Residents ran small factories, schools, clinics and dental practices with no regulation. By 1987 about 33,000 people lived on 2.6 hectares, some 1.2 million per square kilometre. Once Britain and China had agreed on Hong Kong's future in their 1984 Joint Declaration, they could act together, and on 14 January 1987 they announced demolition. Compensating the residents cost HK$2.7 billion. The buildings were pulled down between March 1993 and April 1994.
kowloon-walled-city.mechanism: When two states each decline to use their authority over a place, residents and criminal groups fill the space, but the states' legal claims remain in force and can be used as soon as they agree to act.
kowloon-walled-city.stopped_by: The British and Chinese governments, by a joint decision in 1987
kowloon-walled-city.laws: Almost no government; triads controlled it from the 1950s to the 1970s; unlicensed clinics and schools
kowloon-walled-city.founder: Created by the 1898 lease that left it out; grew through refugees and other residents
kowloon-walled-city.challenge: Survived a 1948 eviction attempt; ended by joint British-Chinese decision
kowloon-walled-city.recognition: Both Britain and China avoided asserting control
kowloon-walled-city.cost: HK$2.7 billion (US$350 million) in compensation to clear residents

liberland.story: Liberland is a self-declared country on a strip of flood-prone land on the Danube river, between Croatia and Serbia. After Yugoslavia broke up, Serbia placed the border on the deepest channel of the river, while Croatia used old land records that follow the river's 19th-century course. That left pockets on the west bank that neither side claims. On 13 April 2015 the Czech politician Vit Jedlicka planted a flag on the largest, 7 square kilometres of floodplain called Gornja Siga, and declared a state where paying tax would be optional. Croatia treats the land as part of an unsettled border dispute, says visitors must obey Croatian law, and has been detaining them since May 2015. Jedlicka spent a night in custody and was fined. In August 2023, after Croatia joined the Schengen area of free travel in Europe, supporters built wooden shelters. Police arrested Jedlicka on 9 September and banned him from Croatia for five years. On 21 September a private company, watched by police, took down and removed the camp, and the settlers moved to houseboats and a village on the Serbian side. Wired magazine reported that 700,000 people had registered support and about 6,000 were paying e-residents, meaning members who hold an online form of citizenship. Nobody lives on the land, and no recognised state accepts it as a country.
liberland.mechanism: A difference between two countries' border claims does not make land free to take, because the country that physically controls it can treat anyone entering as an illegal border crosser, whoever holds title on paper.
liberland.stopped_by: Croatian police, who block access and removed the 2023 camp
liberland.passports: Sold to paying supporters; Wikipedia gives $10,000 and Wired gives $5,000 or equivalent for full citizenship
liberland.challenge: Failed on the ground: Croatia arrested the founder and banned him for five years
liberland.laws: A registry and voting system on a blockchain, an online shared ledger, are planned
liberland.currency: Merit, a cryptocurrency; bitcoin and gold also promoted

neutral-moresnet.story: Neutral Moresnet was a tiny triangle of land between what are now Belgium and Germany that for more than a century belonged to neither of its neighbours. After Napoleon's defeat, the Netherlands and Prussia could not agree who should get a valuable zinc mine there, called Vieille Montagne or Altenberg. On 26 June 1816 they split the Moresnet district in three and left the mine and its village as a neutral area of 3.5 square kilometres, run by one commissioner from each side. Belgium took over the Dutch role after becoming independent in 1830. Napoleon's old legal codes stayed in force, and because the territory had no court of its own, judges from outside came in to hear cases. The mine company dominated daily life, running housing, shops, a hospital and a bank. Taxes were low, there were no import tariffs, and residents counted as stateless, citizens of no country. The population rose from 256 in 1815 to 4,668 in 1914. In 1903 a casino opened and then closed after pressure from Kaiser Wilhelm II. In 1908 the mine doctor Wilhelm Molly proposed making it an Esperanto-speaking state named Amikejo, and a rally for the idea was held on 13 August. Germany invaded Belgium in 1914 and annexed the territory in 1915. The Treaty of Versailles then gave it to Belgium, and from January 1920 it became the Belgian municipality of Kelmis.
neutral-moresnet.mechanism: A place can stay outside either neighbour's rule for generations if both agree to leave it that way, but the arrangement ends when one of them changes its position. This one was a condominium, an area governed jointly by two states.
neutral-moresnet.stopped_by: Germany annexed it in 1915; the Treaty of Versailles then gave it to Belgium
neutral-moresnet.laws: Napoleon's civil and criminal codes, with visiting Belgian and Prussian judges
neutral-moresnet.recognition: Created and run jointly by its neighbouring states
neutral-moresnet.founder: Netherlands and Prussia, by a compromise in 1816
neutral-moresnet.passports: None issued; residents were treated as stateless
neutral-moresnet.challenge: Lasted 104 years, until the First World War ended its neutrality

no-mans-land-cimarron-territory.story: No Man's Land was a strip of the American plains, now the Oklahoma panhandle, that belonged to no state or territory for 40 years. It came about through the politics of slavery. When Texas joined the United States in 1845, federal law barred slavery north of latitude 36 degrees 30 minutes. Under the Compromise of 1850, Texas gave up its land north of that line. Later laws fixed New Mexico's boundary at the 103rd meridian and, in 1854, Kansas's at the 37th parallel. A strip about 170 miles long was left between them, officially called the Public Land Strip. Cattlemen moved in after the Civil War and made their own rules for land and disputes. In 1885 the US Supreme Court ruled that the strip was not part of the neighbouring Cherokee lands. In 1886 Interior Secretary L.Q.C. Lamar declared it public land open to squatters, people who settle without title. Because it had never been officially surveyed, the Homestead Act, which gave settlers free land, could not apply. Thousands came anyway and surveyed their own claims. They set up a government called Cimarron Territory, with its own law code and Owen G. Chase at its head, and asked Congress to recognise it in February and December 1887. Congress did not. In 1890 the strip was joined to the new Oklahoma Territory, and it became part of the state of Oklahoma.
no-mans-land-cimarron-territory.mechanism: Land can lie inside a country's borders and still have no local government. People lived there for decades without valid title, because only Congress could set up a government and legal land system for it.
no-mans-land-cimarron-territory.laws: Settlers surveyed their own claims and wrote their own law code
no-mans-land-cimarron-territory.challenge: Requests to Congress in 1887 for territorial status failed; the strip was absorbed in 1890
no-mans-land-cimarron-territory.founder: Settlers; Owen G. Chase led the 1886-87 Cimarron Territory effort

republic-of-cospaia.story: Cospaia was a tiny republic in central Italy that lasted nearly four centuries because of a mistake in a treaty. In 1440 Pope Eugene IV, short of money, handed the Sansepolcro district to Florence as security for a debt of 25,000 ducats. The treaty set the new border at a creek called the Rio. Two creeks with that name ran about 500 metres apart, and each side took the one nearer to itself, so 330 hectares around the village of Cospaia ended up belonging to neither. Its roughly 250 inhabitants declared themselves independent, with the Latin motto Perpetua et firma libertas, meaning lasting and firm liberty, which is still written over the church door. In 1484 Florence and the Papal States accepted this, finding it cheaper than redrawing the border. Goods passed through free of tariffs. Tobacco reached the area in 1574, and after a papal ban on it in 1624, Cospaia gave its farmland to the crop. The neighbours, by then Tuscany and the Papal States, complained of smugglers and agreed to divide the village in 1826. Fourteen heads of families signed their submission in exchange for a silver coin each and permission to grow up to half a million tobacco plants a year.
republic-of-cospaia.mechanism: A drafting error can produce real independence if both neighbours find it cheaper to tolerate than to fix, but those neighbours can end that tolerance by agreement.
republic-of-cospaia.founder: Local inhabitants, after a treaty drafting error
republic-of-cospaia.stopped_by: Tuscany and the Papal States, by an agreed division in 1826
republic-of-cospaia.challenge: Tolerated for nearly four centuries, then divided by agreement

republic-of-indian-stream.story: Indian Stream was a small self-governing republic from 1832 to 1835 in what is now the far north of New Hampshire, on the border with Canada. The 1783 treaty that ended the American Revolution set the border at the "northwesternmost head of the Connecticut River", and several streams could fit that description. Britain and the United States each claimed the land, and both sent in tax collectors and debt-collecting sheriffs. To stop paying twice, about 300 settlers formed an assembly, declared independence on 9 July 1832 and wrote a constitution that was to last until the two powers settled the border. Luther Parker, one of the drafters, served as Justice of the Peace. The sheriff of Coos County, New Hampshire, kept acting there anyway. On 30 July 1835 he called for the militia, and two infantry companies gathered at nearby Stewartstown. On 4 August he met 30 to 40 assembly members and gave them an ultimatum, and most gave in. The next day five leaders told a British official that help had not come in time and that they had accepted annexation by New Hampshire. That October an arrest over a hardware-store debt led armed locals to shoot a British deputy and capture a magistrate in Canada, and New Hampshire militia occupied the area until February 1836. The area became the town of Pittsburg in 1840, and the Webster-Ashburton Treaty of 1842 gave it to the United States.
republic-of-indian-stream.mechanism: A government set up in a disputed border area lasts only until one of the claiming powers is willing to use force. New Hampshire ended this one with a threat of militia occupation, without firing on it.
republic-of-indian-stream.stopped_by: The Coos County sheriff and New Hampshire militia
republic-of-indian-stream.laws: Written constitution, elected assembly, Justice of the Peace
republic-of-indian-stream.challenge: Gave way under threat of military occupation
republic-of-indian-stream.founder: Assembly of settlers; Luther Parker was one of the constitution's drafters

sapodilla-cayes.story: The Sapodilla Cayes are a small uninhabited atoll, a ring of tiny coral islands, in the Gulf of Honduras, run by Belize as a marine reserve. Three countries have an interest in them, and the dispute is now before the International Court of Justice, the United Nations' top court. Honduras claims them in its 1982 constitution, and Guatemala claims the same territory in its separate case against Belize. On 16 November 2022 Belize took Honduras to the court, saying the cayes have been part of its territory since the early 19th century, first as the settlement of Belize, then as the colony of British Honduras, and since 1981 as an independent state. Guatemala applied on 1 December 2023 for permission to join the case, and hearings on that request ran from 24 to 26 November 2025. On 19 March 2026 the court unanimously allowed Guatemala to intervene as a non-party, meaning it can state its views without being bound as a full party, limited to the cayes and fishing rights around them. It first set written filings for 20 July 2026, and an order of 16 April 2026 extended that deadline. The court has not yet ruled on who owns the cayes.
sapodilla-cayes.mechanism: Even tiny uninhabited land is rarely terra nullius (land belonging to no state). Any claim to it can end up in a case between states at the International Court of Justice.
sapodilla-cayes.founder: Belize, which brought the case at the International Court of Justice
sapodilla-cayes.why: The earlier text gave 20 July 2026 as the filing date. The court's case page lists an order of 16 April 2026 extending that time limit.
sapodilla-cayes.challenge: Case pending at the International Court of Justice

floating-island-french-polynesia.story: The Floating Island Project was a plan to build a floating settlement in a lagoon in French Polynesia, the self-governing French territory in the South Pacific that includes Tahiti. It came from the Seasteading Institute of San Francisco, a group that wants to create new societies on the ocean, with their own rules. The institute chose the territory for its links to France, its autonomy and its calm waters. In January 2017 French Polynesia signed a memorandum of understanding with the institute, a document that records intentions and is usually weaker than a contract. Minister Jean-Christophe Bouissou signed for the territory and executive director Randolph Hencken for the institute, and President Edouard Fritch appeared by video. The deal cleared the way for studies toward "seazones" with a special governing framework, and the institute formed a company, Blue Frontiers, to build the project. It inspected sites near Tahiti, Tupai and Raiatea, and considered the Atimaono lagoon south of Tahiti for its depth and closeness to shore. Local residents objected. Opposition politician Valentina Cross held up a protest poster and asked the government to withdraw, and the ruling Tapura Huiraatira party first said nothing had been signed. On 28 February 2018 RNZ, New Zealand's public broadcaster, reported the government's position that the deal had no legal force, had expired at the end of 2017, and was now void, and no floating island was built.
floating-island-french-polynesia.mechanism: A special legal zone inside a state's waters needs that state's political consent. The memorandum here was not binding, so the government could walk away from it at no cost once locals objected.
floating-island-french-polynesia.stopped_by: French Polynesian government, after local opposition
floating-island-french-polynesia.laws: A planned special legal zone with its own governing rules
floating-island-french-polynesia.challenge: No court case; the government called the agreement void
floating-island-french-polynesia.recognition: French Polynesia signed a non-binding memorandum, later declared void

oceanix-busan.story: Oceanix Busan is a proposed floating neighbourhood off Busan, a port city in South Korea, backed by the city government and UN-Habitat, the United Nations agency for cities. Its stated aim is to give coastal cities new land as seas rise and housing costs grow. UN-Habitat said two of every five people live within 100 kilometres of a coast and that 90 percent of mega cities are vulnerable to rising seas. On 18 November 2021 Busan, UN-Habitat and the company OCEANIX signed an agreement to build a prototype, with about $200 million anticipated as the cost. On 26 April 2022, at UN Headquarters in New York, the three partners unveiled the design for what they called the world's first prototype sustainable floating city, and said they were on track to deliver it. Unlike earlier projects to settle the sea, it would stand in South Korean waters under a city government, with no attempt to leave any state's law. In October 2023 the Busan broadcaster KNN reported that a conference on the project gave no concrete financing or construction plans. No report shows that construction has started or that anyone lives there, and it is listed as not yet built.
oceanix-busan.mechanism: Oceanix uses the same engineering idea as seasteading, floating land, but keeps it inside a country's territory with UN support. Building on the sea and leaving national law are separate things.
oceanix-busan.recognition: Backed by UN-Habitat and the city of Busan; no independence claimed
oceanix-busan.founder: OCEANIX with UN-Habitat and the city of Busan

seapods-panama.story: SeaPods are small floating homes built by the company Ocean Builders at a marina on the Caribbean coast of Panama. Ocean Builders had first tried to live beyond national law. Its 2019 seastead off Phuket was raided by the Thai navy, and its 2020 plan to turn a cruise ship into a floating community, the MS Satoshi, collapsed because no insurer would cover it. It then turned to homes inside a state's waters. In September 2022 the Panamanian newspaper Panamá América reported houses being built at Linton Bay Marina in the province of Colón, designed with the Dutch architect Koen Olthuis and his firm Waterstudio. The company took reservations for a $100 deposit, with prices from about $295,000 to $1.5 million. A SeaPod stands above the water on a float tethered to the seabed by anchors, runs mainly on solar power, collects rain water and carries Starlink satellite internet and more than 100 sensors. At the unveiling on 22 September 2022, in front of an audience that included Panama's president, Laurentino Cortizo, the prototype tipped over with people inside. The company blamed a failed bilge pump, a pump that clears water from the hull, and denied that the home sank, and AP reported no injuries. By June 2023 a Condé Nast Traveler writer stayed in one off Panama's Caribbean coast as among the first guests, and a Smithsonian researcher told the writer that floating pods touch the seabed less than bungalows on pillars. The company does not claim independence from Panama. No report gives a number of permanent residents.
seapods-panama.mechanism: After the Thai navy raid, the same promoters put their homes in a marina in a host country, accepting that country's law and permissions.
seapods-panama.pop: Overnight guests from 2023; number of residents not known
seapods-panama.laws: Sited at a marina in Colón, under Panamanian law
seapods-panama.challenge: Not challenged; it operates inside Panama
seapods-panama.recognition: Not applicable; it is in Panama

add_sources.t: $1.5 million floating home prototype collapses at unveiling event, All That's Interesting

duran-sun.story: María Ángeles Durán, a woman from Vigo in Spain, claims to own the Sun. In 2010 she had a notary record her statement that she owned it, and she threatened to charge people for using solar power. She argues that the international treaty that stops countries from owning a planet or star does not bind individuals. She then sold plots on the Sun on the auction site eBay at one euro per square metre. About two years after she opened her account, eBay removed the listings under its policy on intangible goods and blocked her account. She sued in court number 5 of Alcobendas, near Madrid, seeking 10,000 euros. Reports differ on what the courts did next. A report from June 2015 said a Spanish court recognised her claim and let her pursue the dispute, with a first hearing set for 17 June 2015. The Mexican newspaper Excelsior said in 2022 that the court declared itself competent and gave her standing to sue, and it dated recognition of her ownership to 2012, without citing documents. The Spanish site Genbeta later wrote that the court dismissed her case and that a Spanish court said in 2016 that a person cannot legally own the Sun, but it names no court document and credits Excelsior, whose article does not say this. Letting someone sue is a different thing from finding that she owns the Sun, and no confirmed court ruling says she does.
duran-sun.mechanism: A notary recording a claim only records that it was made, and a court accepting a consumer lawsuit only lets the case go ahead. Neither step makes a person the owner of a star.
duran-sun.stopped_by: eBay's policy against selling intangible goods
duran-sun.challenge: eBay removed her listings; she sued in Alcobendas, and Genbeta reports the case was dismissed, which is unconfirmed

ad-coelum-downward.story: Ad coelum is an old rule of property law about how far land ownership reaches up and down. The Latin phrase cuius est solum, eius est usque ad coelum et ad inferos means "whoever owns the soil, it is theirs all the way to the sky and to the depths". The saying has been traced to the 13th-century Italian lawyer Accursius and is said to date in English law to the time of King Edward I. William Blackstone gave it its broad form in his Commentaries on the Laws of England in 1766. Modern law keeps only a limited version. Above the ground, an owner controls the space close to the land and cannot stop flights far overhead. Below the ground, an owner holds rights to what is underneath, but in some places minerals beyond a set depth are separate from the land title, and the state often owns them permanently and leases them out. The rule matters to anyone hoping to escape national law by going underground. It settles who owns a chamber or mine shaft under a plot of land, and that owner still holds it under the law of the country it lies in.
ad-coelum-downward.mechanism: Land ownership reaches downward only as far as the law allows, so anything dug beneath a plot stays part of the same property and the same country.
ad-coelum-downward.founder: Traced to the lawyer Accursius in the 13th century; stated broadly by William Blackstone in 1766

cyberbunker.story: CyberBunker was a web-hosting business run from former military bunkers in the Netherlands and Germany, which called itself an independent republic. In 1995 Herman-Johan Xennt bought a 20,000-square-foot former NATO bunker near Kloetinge in the Netherlands, built in 1955 to survive a nuclear attack. He hosted any website except those with child abuse material or terrorism. Its spokesman, Sven Olaf Kamphuis, called it the Republic of CyberBunker and styled himself Minister of Telecommunications and Foreign Affairs. In 2002 a fire exposed a laboratory making the drug MDMA, three men were jailed, and the town refused a business licence. The firm moved its servers above ground and kept advertising the bunker. A Hamburg court barred it from hosting the file-sharing site The Pirate Bay in 2010, and Dutch prosecutors had Kamphuis arrested in Spain in 2013 over a computer attack on the anti-spam group Spamhaus. That year it bought a second bunker at Traben-Trarbach in Germany. Investigators tapped its traffic from 2015 and sent in undercover officers posing as a gardener and a cleaner. In September 2019, 600 police raided it. In late 2021 the regional court in Trier convicted all eight defendants, including Xennt, of belonging to a criminal organisation, but not of aiding their customers' crimes. Sentences ran from one suspended year to five years and nine months. In 2023 Germany's Federal Court of Justice largely upheld the verdict.
cyberbunker.mechanism: Calling a bunker a republic gives it no legal status. The country it stood in applied its licensing, wiretapping and criminal law to everything inside.
cyberbunker.laws: Its own rule: any website except child abuse material and terrorism
cyberbunker.stopped_by: German police raid in September 2019, and convictions in 2021
cyberbunker.challenge: Lost in a Hamburg court in 2010; convicted in Germany in 2021

pionen-bahnhof.story: Pionen is a data centre, a building full of computer servers, inside a former wartime shelter under the city of Stockholm, Sweden. The shelter was built in 1943 in the White Mountains in the Södermalm district to protect government functions in wartime. The Swedish internet provider Bahnhof converted it, and it opened on 11 September 2008. It lies under 30 metres of granite, behind a door 40 centimetres thick, can be reached only by an entrance tunnel, and is described as able to withstand a hydrogen bomb. It covers 1,100 square metres and has greenhouses, fountains, simulated daylight and a large saltwater fish tank. Its two backup generators are submarine engines. Bahnhof also rents space there to others, and in 2010 the document-leaking organisation WikiLeaks kept servers on the site. HavenCo, a company on the self-declared sea fort of Sealand, sold a similar hardened home for data, and it relied on a claim of independence. Pionen makes no such claim. It stands at Renstiernas gata 35 and 37 in central Stockholm, and Swedish government and law apply to it as to any other business.
pionen-bahnhof.mechanism: A hardened site protects servers from physical harm. Its legal protection comes entirely from the law of the country it stands in.

survival-condo.story: Survival Condo is a luxury underground bunker for rich people preparing for disaster, built inside an old missile silo in Kansas. In 2008 Larry Hall bought a disused Atlas missile silo at Raven Ridge near Concordia for $300,000. It goes down 197 feet. He built a 15-floor bunker with 12 condominium units for up to 75 people, plus a swimming pool, theatre, library, gym, climbing wall, vegetable gardens, fish tanks and three years of stored food. It also has armouries, a sniper post with a remote-controlled rifle and a jail cell. Building finished by 2012 at a cost of $20 million. Hall said all units had sold by 2017, though 6 appeared for sale in 2020, and no owners were living there that year. Ordinary law applied to it as it does anywhere. Peter Ziegler, who bought Unit 5 in 2013, lent the company $3 million. After he died in 2017, his estate sued in January 2019, saying assets had been moved to other companies, and the two sides settled that August. The facility is owned by a Kansas not-for-profit company, incorporated in 2012.
survival-condo.mechanism: Buying a missile silo gives ordinary ownership of land in Kansas, so debts, lawsuits and courts reach the bunker as they reach any other property.
survival-condo.cost: Silo bought for $300,000; about $20 million to develop
survival-condo.pop: Room for up to 75; no owners were living there in 2020
survival-condo.recognition: Ordinary Kansas real estate, owned by a not-for-profit company

unclos-shelf-subsoil.story: The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the main treaty on the oceans, sets out who controls the rock under the sea near a country's coast. The rules are in its section on the continental shelf, the shallow sea floor that extends from a country's land. Article 76 defines the shelf as the seabed and subsoil beyond the territorial sea, the belt of water a country fully controls. It runs out to the edge of the continental margin, or to 200 nautical miles from the coast where the margin stops short. Article 77 gives the coastal country sovereign rights to explore the shelf and take its natural resources, including minerals in the subsoil. These rights are exclusive, so if the country leaves them unused, nobody else may use them without its express consent. Article 85 adds that nothing in this part limits a coastal country's right to exploit the subsoil by tunnelling, however deep the water above. The deep ocean floor and its subsoil are not part of the shelf. Together these articles mean the coastal country's rights in the shelf subsoil hold even where the water above is open to everyone, so a private mining shaft there would need its consent.
unclos-shelf-subsoil.mechanism: Beyond the territorial sea, the rock under the continental shelf stays under the coastal country's exclusive control, including by tunnel, even where the water above is free to all.
unclos-shelf-subsoil.founder: Countries that are parties to the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea

vivos-shelters.story: Vivos is a California company, founded by Robert Vicino, that sells places in underground shelters for use after a disaster. Its first completed shelter, in Indiana, dates from the Cold War, was built to withstand a near direct hit from a 20-megaton bomb, and holds 80 people. In 2016 the company took over shelters built in 1967 at the former Black Hills Ordnance Depot in South Dakota, where it lists 575 bunkers of about 2,150 square feet each. It also planned to convert a Soviet-built complex at Rothenstein in Germany for 1,000 people, where fire rules were expected to require sprinklers throughout. In 2013 Vivos acquired rights to buy part of a former limestone mine at Atchison, Kansas, once owned by the US Army, for 5,000 people. It cancelled that in June 2014 after Army geologists raised concerns about collapses. In September 2022 Vicino said the firm had about 100,000 members and over 1,000 buyers, figures that come from the company.
vivos-shelters.mechanism: Vivos sells underground space as ordinary property, so German fire codes and US geological reviews apply to it as they would to any building above ground.
vivos-shelters.pop: The company claims about 100,000 members and over 1,000 buyers (September 2022)

aquarius-reef-base.story: Aquarius is an underwater research laboratory on the sea floor off Florida, where scientists live for days at a time. It sits 62 feet down next to Conch Reef, 5.4 miles off Key Largo, in the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, a protected area run by the US government. Crews use saturation diving. After staying under pressure, their bodies reach a steady state, so they can work outside for up to nine hours a day and need to decompress only once, at the end of the mission. Research has ranged from coral disease to the way nutrients move through the reef, and NASA uses the base to train astronauts for spacewalks and lunar missions. It was built in Victoria, Texas, in 1986, first worked in the US Virgin Islands, and was placed in the Keys in 1993.
