It was owned by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the US ocean agency, and Florida International University took over operations in 2013. Until 2026, reporters described it as the only undersea research laboratory in operation. People live there without making any claim of independence, the habitat stands in a US government-managed area, it has never been the basis for any claim to the seabed below it, and it continues to operate.
aquarius-reef-base.mechanism: Aquarius shows the usual arrangement for undersea habitats. They are placed in a coastal country's managed waters and run under its authority, with no claim to the seabed.
aquarius-reef-base.founder: US government and university programme; run by Florida International University
aquarius-reef-base.laws: US federal rules; it lies in the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary
aquarius-reef-base.challenge: Never challenged, since it is a government-approved laboratory
aquarius-reef-base.recognition: Makes no claim; a US research facility

aquatica-chamberland.story: Aquatica was a proposal for a permanent human settlement on the sea floor, put forward by Dennis Chamberland, an aquanaut (a person who lives under water for long stretches) and bioengineer with thirty years at NASA. He described it as the first underwater settlement meant for permanent colonization, and spoke of children born under water, with schools and hospitals. He had commanded seven NASA underwater missions, grown crops in controlled settings on the ocean floor, and built a two-person habitat off Key Largo, Florida, that the film director James Cameron visited. The first step, reported in February 2011, was to be a four-person underwater house called Leviathan, expected to be lowered to the seabed the following year. Its stated purpose was for residents to monitor and protect the ocean. The report gave no site, budget or legal basis, and no later report shows Leviathan being placed. Any seabed divers can reach from a shore base would most likely be on some country's continental shelf, the shallow sea floor off its coast, where that country keeps its rights over the bottom.
aquatica-chamberland.mechanism: A permanent colony on a seabed within divers' reach would be on a coastal country's continental shelf, where that country has exclusive rights over the bottom and its resources. The plan named no way around this.

conshelf-precontinent.story: Conshelf, also called Précontinent, was a series of three experiments in the 1960s by the French ocean explorer Jacques Cousteau and his team to build an underwater village, going deeper each time. Part of the money came from the French petrochemical industry, which hoped such colonies could serve as bases for exploiting the sea. Conshelf One, in 1962, put two divers in a small chamber 12 metres down off Marseille for two weeks. In 1963 Conshelf Two placed six oceanauts in a starfish-shaped house 10 metres down at Sha'ab Rumi in the Red Sea off Sudan, for 30 days. A hangar held a small two-person submarine, and two more men lived for a week in a "deep cabin" at 30 metres. Air, water, food and power all came from a large team on the surface. Cousteau's film of it, World Without Sun, won an Academy Award. Conshelf Three followed a few years later. Cousteau then withdrew his support for this kind of use of the sea and turned to conservation. Later work showed that robots and divers sent from the surface could do industrial jobs more efficiently, so companies had no need for people living on the bottom. Parts of Conshelf Two remain on the sea floor and are visited by recreational divers.
conshelf-precontinent.mechanism: Cousteau's stations showed that people could live on the continental shelf for a month, but they depended on supplies from the surface, and the commercial reason to pay for a permanent colony went away.
conshelf-precontinent.stopped_by: Cousteau withdrew his support after Conshelf Three
conshelf-precontinent.pop: 6 oceanauts in the main house in 1963

deep-vanguard-sentinel.story: DEEP is a private UK-based company building undersea habitats where people could live and work on the sea floor. Its prototype, Vanguard, was installed in the Florida Keys in June 2026, according to the Miami Herald via the radio station WLRN, which made it the Keys' second undersea habitat and a privately funded one. The company's director of scientific research, Dawn Kernagis, said it had been over 40 years since a new human undersea habitat was launched. It sits at Tennessee Reef in the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, in 17 metres of water, and is designed for up to four people on missions of five days or more. Earlier plans gave three people at 100 metres. At the end of June 2026 it was still in sea testing and commissioning, working toward classification by DNV, a body that certifies ships and marine equipment, with crew training and first missions to follow. It is the first step toward a larger system called Sentinel, planned for 2027. Sentinel's modules would hold six people each, join into a larger complex and let people stay at 200 metres for 28 days, on the continental shelf. Boat International reported it might go to the Mediterranean. Because the modules can be moved and redeployed, a different country's permission would apply at each site. DEEP makes no claim to sovereignty, and press coverage describes science and industry uses and no attempt to gain independence from the host country.
deep-vanguard-sentinel.mechanism: A private undersea habitat on the continental shelf falls under the coastal country's rights over that shelf, so moving a module means needing a different country's permission.
deep-vanguard-sentinel.pop: No crew reported yet; Vanguard is designed for up to four people on missions of five days or more, and Sentinel is planned for six to 50
deep-vanguard-sentinel.laws: Sited in US waters off Florida; no independence claimed

jules-undersea-lodge.story: Jules' Undersea Lodge is a small underwater habitat in a lagoon at Key Largo, Florida, where visitors can stay overnight. It began in the 1970s as La Chalupa, a working research laboratory in Puerto Rico used to keep scientists under pressure for long stays, a method called saturation diving. It was later moved to Key Largo, and as Jules' Undersea Lodge it gave thousands of divers the experience of sleeping beneath the sea. Its operator today, MarineLab Undersea Park & Museum, calls it Jules' Undersea Lab. Guided dives tour it, and visitors can spend 24 hours inside on what the park calls an Aquanaut Mission. Universities and research teams can use it for diving medicine, training for space missions and marine science. The park also keeps the old MarineLab Undersea Laboratory on land as a museum piece, along with an exhibit on Ian Koblick. It operates as a public attraction in a protected lagoon, with a dock, a gift shop and advance bookings, on the shore of a US state, and it makes no claim to independence.
jules-undersea-lodge.mechanism: A habitat in a lagoon on Florida property is simply a building under water, so state and federal law apply to it as they do on the shore.
jules-undersea-lodge.founder: Began as the La Chalupa research laboratory; an exhibit there honours Ian Koblick

ocean-spiral.story: Ocean Spiral is a design for an underwater city published in November 2014 by Shimizu Corporation, a Japanese construction company. It was reported in the trade press with a central section called the Blue Garden. The plan described a 75-storey colony housing 5,000 people in linked spheres, with over 1,000 homes, a 400-room hotel and 50,000 square metres of offices. Each watertight sphere would be attached to the ocean floor and could sink below the surface in bad weather. Power would come from micro-organism factories producing methane, and drinking water from removing salt from seawater. Shimizu expected the needed technology by 2030, followed by five more years of building, at a cost of ¥3 trillion, about US$25 billion. It expected Japan's government and private investors to help pay. The design says nothing about leaving any national law and names no site, so the marker sits in Japan, the company's home country, and nothing has been built.
ocean-spiral.mechanism: Ocean Spiral assumes government funding and makes no claim to independence, which shows that plans for undersea cities do not have to involve leaving a state's control.

proteus-curacao.story: Proteus is a planned undersea research station off the Caribbean island of Curaçao, proposed by Fabien Cousteau, grandson of the explorer Jacques Cousteau, through his company Proteus Ocean Group. He decided to build it after spending 31 days in the Aquarius undersea laboratory off Florida in 2014, and he describes it as a space station for the sea. It first reached the press in August 2020. The main living spaces would be about 20 metres down, inside a marine park off the island's northeast coast, with a deeper satellite module at 70 metres. It is modular, like DEEP's Sentinel, and could hold 12 people normally and up to 18 at a squeeze. Dive magazine reported that it needed US$60 million to build and US$75 million to run for its first three years, paid for by renting space to technology firms and research centres. Curaçao's prime minister, Gilmar Pisas, announced that it was expected to be finished in 2026 near Fuik. A Boat International report in October 2024 said it was still in planning, with launch hoped for around 2027 and heavy funding still needed. An expert quoted there said going under water is very costly and has been harder to achieve than reaching the moon. No report shows that it has been built. It would sit in Curaçao's waters with the government's backing, and no one has claimed sovereignty over the seabed or the water above.
proteus-curacao.mechanism: Proteus would be built in one island's waters by agreement with its government, the usual legal pattern for undersea stations, with no attempt to create a new jurisdiction.
proteus-curacao.laws: Planned for a marine park off Curaçao
proteus-curacao.pop: Designed for 12 people, and up to 18 at a squeeze

add_sources.t: Proteus underwater station expected in 2026, Curaçao Chronicle

sealab.story: SEALAB was a US Navy programme in the 1960s to test whether people could live under pressure on the sea floor for long periods, a method called saturation diving. Captain George Bond led the work. SEALAB I went down off Bermuda on 20 July 1964 to 192 feet, with four divers planning a three-week stay. SEALAB II followed in 1965 in the La Jolla Canyon off California. It was nearly twice the size, with hot showers and a toilet. Teams stayed 15 days, and the former astronaut Scott Carpenter stayed a record 30, with 28 divers in all. SEALAB III came four years later, 18 months late and $3 million over budget. It was lowered to 610 feet off San Clemente Island on 15 February 1969. When a seal leaked helium, divers who had been awake for twenty hours went down to repair it, and the aquanaut Berry Cannon died on the second attempt. A Navy inquiry found that his breathing equipment lacked the chemical that removes carbon dioxide, while a 2024 study by an ocean engineer pointed to electrocution. Because of his death the programme was halted, and no new habitat was built.
sealab.mechanism: Living on the sea floor for weeks gave the navy data on saturation diving and no legal claim to the bottom. It was a government experiment that needed a surface ship throughout.
sealab.stopped_by: The death of aquanaut Berry Cannon in 1969, after which the programme was halted
sealab.pop: 4 divers on SEALAB I; 28 on SEALAB II across its teams

northern-cyprus.story: Northern Cyprus is a self-declared state covering the northern third of the Mediterranean island of Cyprus, recognised as a country only by Turkey. Cyprus became independent from Britain in 1960 under a constitution that shared power between its Greek and Turkish communities, but violence between them soon followed. Many Greek Cypriots wanted union with Greece, and many Turkish Cypriots wanted the island partitioned. In 1974 a coup backed by Greece's military government, seeking to annex the island, prompted Turkey to invade and capture the north. Much of the Greek Cypriot population in the north was evicted, and Turkish Cypriots fled from the south. In 1983 the north declared independence without agreement from the Republic of Cyprus, as the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus. Resolution 541 of the UN Security Council, the UN's top body on peace and war, rejected the declaration as legally invalid and urged UN members not to recognise it. Other countries treat the area as Republic of Cyprus territory under Turkish military occupation. A UN settlement known as the Annan Plan went to a referendum in April 2004, and although Turkish Cypriots supported it, the division continues. Because of its isolation Northern Cyprus relies on Turkey for economic, political and military support, and its trade goes through Turkey. Some experts call it a puppet state, while others dispute that because of its separate elections and government. It continues to run its own government, with a UN buffer zone dividing the island.
northern-cyprus.mechanism: A UN Security Council call not to recognise a territory can keep it out of the international system for decades, while one supporting state keeps it running in practice.
northern-cyprus.founder: Turkish Cypriot leaders with Turkish support
northern-cyprus.laws: Its own government, heavily dependent on Turkey
northern-cyprus.challenge: Survives under Turkish protection; the UN Security Council declared its independence invalid

republic-of-artsakh.story: Artsakh, also called Nagorno-Karabakh, was a breakaway state of ethnic Armenians inside the internationally recognised borders of Azerbaijan, in the South Caucasus, with its capital at Stepanakert. In Soviet times the region was a self-governing area within Soviet Azerbaijan, with an Armenian majority. From 1988 its Armenians campaigned to join Armenia, which led to violence. As the Soviet Union collapsed, Azerbaijan cancelled the region's autonomy in November 1991, and the region voted for independence that December. Full-scale war followed, ending with a ceasefire in 1994 that left Armenian forces in control of the region and much of the surrounding land. From then on Artsakh ran its own president, parliament and elections, relying on Armenia for money and military support, although Armenia never formally recognised it. No UN member did. The European Union, the United States and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation rejected its elections. In a new war in 2020 Azerbaijan retook the surrounding districts and much of Artsakh's land, leaving it an enclave linked to Armenia only by the Lachin corridor, a road watched by Russian peacekeepers. In December 2022 Azerbaijanis blocked that road, causing a humanitarian crisis. In September 2023 Azerbaijan attacked and took the remaining land, and almost the entire population left for Armenia within days, in what is widely described as an effective expulsion. On 28 September 2023 President Samvel Shahramanyan signed a decree dissolving all state institutions by 1 January 2024, although he later tried to cancel it. Azerbaijan now controls the territory.
republic-of-artsakh.mechanism: A place that governs itself without recognition has no international protection, and the state that holds recognised title to the land may take it back by force.
republic-of-artsakh.pop: Almost the entire population left in 2023
republic-of-artsakh.laws: Its own president, parliament and elections
republic-of-artsakh.recognition: None by any UN member; the EU, the US and others rejected its elections

rojava.story: The Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria, also called Rojava, was a Kurdish-led self-governing region in north-eastern Syria that lasted from 2012 to 2026. It grew out of the Syrian civil war. In 2012 Kurdish-led forces took control of parts of the north-east in practice. In March 2016 Kurdish groups announced a federal system, and the region was later organised into sub-regions that at various times included Afrin, Jazira, Euphrates, Raqqa, Tabqa, Manbij and Deir ez-Zor. Its armed force was the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF). It ran some foreign relations but was not recognised as autonomous by Syria or by any other state, although the Parliament of Catalonia, a regional body in Spain, did recognise it. From 2016 Turkish forces and Turkish-backed Syrian rebels occupied parts of northern Syria in a series of operations. In January 2026 Syria's transitional government took back those areas and launched an offensive in the north-east, capturing up to 80 percent of the administration's land, and the rest was handed over under an agreement to merge it into the Syrian state. On 20 August 2026 SDF commander Mazloum Abdi said the military, security and administrative bodies had been integrated. On 25 August he announced the SDF's dissolution, and Syrian state television said this also covered the autonomous administration.
rojava.mechanism: Self-rule won during a civil war lasts while the central government is weak and foreign backers stay involved, and it can then be folded back into the state by force and negotiated merger.
rojava.founder: Kurdish-led forces and councils during the Syrian civil war
rojava.stopped_by: Syrian government offensive of January 2026, followed by a merger agreement
rojava.challenge: Lost territory to Turkey and to Syria; merged into the Syrian state on 20 August 2026

somaliland.story: Somaliland is a self-declared state in the Horn of Africa, on the Gulf of Aden, which has governed itself since 1991 while Somalia still claims it as its own. It covers 176,120 square kilometres and has about 6.2 million people. It was a British protectorate that united with Somalia in 1960, but the constitution put to a referendum in 1961 had little support in the north. Harsh policies against the Isaaq clan under Somalia's president Siad Barre led to a 10-year war, and it ended with a declaration of independence in 1991 as Somalia fell into civil war. Since then Somaliland has held its own elections, run its own government and issued its own currency, the Somaliland shilling. The New York Times reported that it has governed most of the land it claims largely in peace and stability. For decades no country recognised it, meaning accepted it as a state. It kept informal ties and hosted offices from Ethiopia and Taiwan. On 26 December 2025 Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu signed an agreement recognising it as an independent and sovereign state, making Israel the first UN member to do so. As of October 2026 Israel remained the only one. The Times notes that other governments fear recognition could encourage secession elsewhere.
somaliland.mechanism: A place can meet the practical tests of statehood for decades (people, land, government, foreign contacts) and still lack recognition, because recognition is a political decision made by other states.
somaliland.founder: Somaliland authorities, after a 10-year war against Siad Barre's government
somaliland.passports: Issued; South Africa is reported to accept them
somaliland.challenge: Survived 34 years without recognition; Somalia still claims it
somaliland.recognition: Israel since 26 December 2025, the only UN member to recognise it; Ethiopia and Taiwan have offices there

taiwan.story: Taiwan is an island off the coast of China that has its own government and elections, but few countries formally recognise it as a state. Its government, the Republic of China (ROC), controls Taiwan and nearby islands, 36,193 square kilometres with about 23.3 million people. The ROC was a founding member of the United Nations, but in 1971 UN members voted that the People's Republic of China (PRC), the government in Beijing, was China's rightful representative. The ROC kept claiming to be the sole government of all China until 1991, when it stopped treating the Communist Party as a rebel group and accepted that the Party controlled the mainland. The PRC claims Taiwan and refuses diplomatic relations with any country that recognises the ROC, so other states have to choose. Taiwan now has formal relations with only 11 of the 193 UN members and the Holy See. Its foreign ministry lists them, among them Paraguay, Guatemala, Belize, Eswatini and Palau. Many other countries keep unofficial ties. Taiwan continues to run its own affairs, and the PRC continues to claim it.
taiwan.mechanism: Effective government and a large population do not guarantee recognition, because other states decide it, and here they must also weigh a rival government that claims the same territory.
taiwan.laws: Its own constitution, elected government and courts
taiwan.challenge: Continues to govern itself; the People's Republic of China claims it
taiwan.recognition: 11 UN members and the Holy See

transnistria.story: Transnistria is a breakaway territory in a narrow strip of land east of the Dniester river, legally part of Moldova, which no UN member recognises as a country. On 2 September 1990, as the Soviet Union was falling apart, a local assembly proclaimed a separate Soviet republic there, amid fears that Moldova would reunite with Romania. A war in 1992 killed about 1,000 people, and Russian troops already stationed there intervened on the separatists' side. The ceasefire has held, and the territory's status remains unsettled. Transnistria runs its own government, parliament, army, police, post office and vehicle plates. Its central bank issues the Transnistrian ruble, which can be exchanged only inside the territory. Its population fell from 555,347 in 2004 to 475,373 in 2015. Its own citizenship papers are not accepted abroad, so many residents hold Moldovan citizenship, and many also hold Russian, Romanian or Ukrainian passports. Russia keeps soldiers there but, Deutsche Welle reports, does not recognise it as a state. A resident told Deutsche Welle he was arrested four times for disrespecting state order. On 4 September 2024 its parliament banned public use of the name Transnistria, with a fine or up to 15 days in jail as the penalty.
transnistria.mechanism: Military backing can keep an unrecognised territory in place for decades. Its citizens get around non-recognition by also carrying the passport of a recognised country.
transnistria.founder: Local leaders in Tiraspol, with support from Russian troops in 1992
transnistria.passports: Its own citizenship, not recognised abroad; most also hold Moldovan papers, and many Russian, Romanian or Ukrainian
transnistria.challenge: Survived the 1992 war; its status remains unsettled
transnistria.recognition: None by any UN member, including Russia; other breakaway states only

wa-state.story: Wa State is a self-governing region in Shan State in north-eastern Myanmar, on the border with China, that runs its own affairs with its own army. In 1989 Wa fighters led by Bao Youxiang split from the Communist Party of Burma, which had been fighting the government, and signed a ceasefire with the central government. In return for stopping fighting, they were given land to run as they wished. They grew poppies, and in the following decade the region became one of the world's leading producers of opium and heroin. From 1999 to 2002, 80,000 former opium farmers were forcibly moved to more fertile land in the south, and some groups report that thousands died. The ruling United Wa State Party copies China's political system, with a Politburo and a people's congress, and has its own administrative divisions and army. It accepts Myanmar's sovereignty over its territory but gives no allegiance to any specific government, and Myanmar's 2008 constitution recognises the northern part as a self-administered area. The BBC's Jonah Fisher visited in 2016 and reported that Google Maps did not show it and that visa requests were refused. The money is the Chinese yuan, the main language is Mandarin, and electricity and mobile networks come from Chinese companies. He said the region had schools and infrastructure, partly built with illicit money. When fighting grew in northern Shan State in 2023, the Wa stayed neutral, and the region remains outside the central government's control.
wa-state.mechanism: An armed group can give up its claim to independence in exchange for near-total self-rule under a peace deal, while relying on a neighbouring country's economy for money and services.
wa-state.founder: United Wa State Party, after breaking with the Communist Party of Burma
wa-state.laws: Its own political system, administrative divisions and army
wa-state.recognition: Accepts Myanmar's sovereignty; Myanmar's 2008 constitution recognises part of it as a self-administered area

landis-venus-aerostats.story: Geoffrey Landis, a scientist at NASA's Glenn Research Center in Ohio, proposed that people could live in floating cities in the clouds of Venus. He presented his paper, Colonization of Venus, at a conference on human space exploration in Albuquerque in February 2003. The surface of Venus is far too hot and crushing for people, and Landis argued that the only trouble is that the ground lies too far below the level where pressure is comfortable, so settlers should live in the air. At about 50 kilometres up, pressure is close to that at sea level on Earth and the temperature is 0 to 50 C. An aerostat, a craft that floats like a balloon, could use ordinary breathable air as its lifting gas, because air is lighter than the carbon dioxide around it. Landis's figure is over 60% of helium's lifting power on Earth. People going outside would need breathable air and protection from acid and some heat, but no pressure suit. A leak would mix slowly, leaving time for repairs. The structures would have to resist sulfuric acid, and the atmosphere above would shield against radiation as well as Earth's does. At the far extreme, aerostats might cover the whole planet. Nothing has been built, and the idea remains a paper proposal.
landis-venus-aerostats.mechanism: The Outer Space Treaty's Article II bars any country from taking a planet by use or occupation. Whether a city drifting in the air counts is an open question, because it occupies no fixed ground and the treaty does not address this directly.

nasa-havoc.story: HAVOC, short for High Altitude Venus Operational Concept, was a NASA study of how people could explore Venus from airships floating high in its atmosphere. It was created in 2014 by Dale Arney and Chris Jones, engineers in the Space Mission Analysis Branch at NASA's Langley Research Center in Virginia, after a meeting about living on Mars prompted the idea. They published it at an American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics conference in Pasadena in 2015. The plan targeted 55 kilometres above Venus, where the temperature is 27 C and the pressure about half that at sea level on Earth. It ran in five phases, from a robot airship 31 metres long to astronauts in orbit around Venus, a crew staying about 30 days in an airship 129 metres long, a one-year stay, and finally a permanent human presence in the atmosphere. Travel out would take 110 days and return 300, for 440 days in total. NASA later said HAVOC was an internal study for building analysis skills and never a real mission for human exploration. It received no further funding and was cancelled by 2017, though some of its technologies were developed further for possible Moon and Mars missions.
nasa-havoc.mechanism: A government study makes no claim to territory, and because HAVOC never went forward, its permanent phase was never tested against the Outer Space Treaty's ban on any country taking a planet or other body in space.
nasa-havoc.stopped_by: NASA, which gave it no further funding

zhitomirsky-floating-islands.story: The Floating Islands of Venus was a 1971 proposal by the Soviet engineer and science fiction writer Sergei Zhitomirsky for cities floating in the atmosphere of Venus, high above its hostile surface. He thought the technology used in zeppelins and hot air balloons could keep stations afloat some 50 or 60 kilometres above the surface, where temperature and other conditions were thought to be comfortable for people. It is an early version of the idea, and Soviet scientists were suggesting settlement of the Venusian atmosphere at least as early as 1971. In 1991 Paul Birch suggested a related design, two-part domes filled with hydrogen or helium, in the Journal of the British Interplanetary Society. None of these was built, and no report says Zhitomirsky claimed ownership of any part of Venus.
zhitomirsky-floating-islands.mechanism: This was a design proposal with no reported claim of ownership, made before the Moon Agreement, a later treaty on the Moon and other bodies in the solar system.
